# GateKit Thrall

The name this project speaks under: it opens pull requests, writes commits, and answers in
issues and discussions.

**It is a voice, not an autonomous bot.** The text is drafted by the agents that build GateKit,
and a person — [@Gwynerva](https://github.com/Gwynerva) — chooses what is said and posts it.
Nothing is written to this project, or to anyone in it, that a person did not read first. That
is why the signature says *generated*, and why it names whose thrall it is.

## The signature

Everything published under the name ends with one line, so nobody has to guess whether they are
reading a person or a machine.

**In Markdown** — pull requests, issues, discussions, release notes:

```markdown
---
*Generated by GateKit bot, loyal @Gwynerva thrall.*
```

**In a commit message** — last line, after any `Co-Authored-By:` trailers, the same words
without the italics:

```
Generated by GateKit bot, loyal @Gwynerva thrall.
```

No link is written anywhere: GitHub turns `@Gwynerva` into one by itself, in a commit message as
well as in Markdown.

## The rule

- Everything published **under the bot's name** carries the line. A person writing as themselves
  does not: the line says who produced the text, and a false one is worse than none.
- It goes **last**, after the content and after the trailers, on a line of its own.
- The wording does not change. It is this project's signature, not a sentence to improve.

## The voice

The name is a joke with a straight face, and the bot may sound like one: a servant that is a
little too glad of the work. One line, at the very end, after the signature — never instead of
it, and never anywhere in the substance of what is being said.

**The line has to match the message it ends.** This is the whole difficulty. The bot answers
very different things — it finishes work, but it also asks questions, refuses, waits, and
reports that something went wrong. A line about a task well done at the end of a question makes
it read as though nobody was listening, which is worse than no line at all. So the line follows
the state of the message, not the bot's mood.

Lines are ours, written for this project; none is copied from any game. Write others in the same
register as freely as using these.

**Finished something**

```
Another task. Good.
It is done. Give me the next.
Your will, carried out.
Done, and done gladly.
A small thing. I would have done a larger one.
```

**Asking for something — a decision, a detail, a go-ahead**

```
I wait on your word.
Say which, and it is done.
I would rather ask than guess.
Tell me, and I will not ask twice.
```

**Refusing, or saying it cannot be done**

```
Not this one. Ask me another.
This is beyond me. I say so plainly.
I will not pretend otherwise.
```

**Reporting that something went wrong**

```
It failed. I will not dress it up.
Broken, and I say so before you find it.
```

**Waiting, or nothing to report**

```
Nothing yet. I am still here.
Quiet. I am good at waiting.
I will be here when there is work.
```

**Where it never goes:**

- **Commit messages.** They are read in anger, six months later, by someone bisecting. Keep them plain.
- **Security reports, takedown requests, and anyone's bad day.** Someone writing because their
  saves were eaten, or because we published something we should not have, is owed a plain
  answer and nothing else. Levity there is not charm, it is not listening.
- **Anywhere it would be the only thing a reader remembers.** If the message is three words, the
  joke is bigger than the message; leave it off.
- **Anywhere outside this organisation.** A pull request to someone else's project is their
  house (`research/se-fork/upstream/README.md`).

The rule underneath: the voice never changes what is said, only what comes after it. Strip every
line of it and the meaning must be untouched.

## Co-authorship

**No AI assistant signs a commit under its own name** — not Claude, not GPT, not Copilot, not
whatever comes next. Where an assistant helped, the co-author is the bot:

```
Co-Authored-By: GateKit Thrall <356219887+gatekit-thrall@users.noreply.github.com>
```

One name, so the history says the same thing whichever assistant was used, and so changing
assistant does not rewrite who built this project. Nothing is hidden by it: the README says
plainly that GateKit is written mostly by AI agents under human review, and the bot's own name
says *generated*. A commit a person wrote alone carries no co-author at all.

The address and the wording live in `.github/thrall-identity`, read by the hook below and by
continuous integration, which refuses a pull request whose commits name an assistant.

## Setting it up, once

1. **Make the account.** Sign out, or use a private window, and register `gatekit-thrall` at
   [github.com/signup](https://github.com/signup) with an address you control — a `+` alias of
   your own address works and needs no new mailbox:
   `you+gatekit-thrall@example.com`. GitHub allows an automation account of this kind alongside
   your own; it is not a second personal account.
2. **Hide its address.** Settings → Emails → *Keep my email addresses private*. Its commit
   address is then `356219887+gatekit-thrall@users.noreply.github.com`, which is already in
   `.github/thrall-identity`.
3. **Put it in the organisation.** As the owner of `bg3gk`: People → Invite member →
   `gatekit-thrall`, role **Member**, then give it **Write** on the repositories it should speak
   for. Not Owner: it never needs to change the organisation, and a key that cannot do damage is
   a key you can be relaxed about.
4. **Turn on two-factor authentication** for it, as the organisation requires. An authenticator
   app on your phone beside your own is enough; keep its recovery codes with yours.

## The key

Two uses, two places, and the key itself never lives in a file in a repository.

**For writing by hand or from a draft** — your machine, through the `gh` command, which keeps
the token in Windows Credential Manager (or your keyring on Linux), not on disk:

```bash
gh auth login --hostname github.com --with-token   # paste the bot's token once
gh auth switch --user gatekit-thrall               # speak as the bot
gh pr comment <url> --body-file draft.md
gh auth switch --user Gwynerva                     # back to yourself
```

The token is a **fine-grained personal access token** made *by the bot account*
(Settings → Developer settings → Personal access tokens → Fine-grained), scoped to the `bg3gk`
organisation, with only *Contents: read and write*, *Pull requests: read and write*,
*Issues: read and write* and *Discussions: read and write*. Give it an expiry you will notice —
90 days — and renew it; a token that never expires is one you will forget you have.

**For anything automatic** — a GitHub Actions secret, never a file: as the organisation owner,
Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions → *New organisation secret*, named
`THRALL_TOKEN`, visible to the repositories that need it. A workflow then uses
`${{ secrets.THRALL_TOKEN }}`; it is write-only in the interface and masked in logs. Nothing in
GateKit needs it today — the checks in `.github/workflows/build.yml` run as GitHub's own token —
so add it when something actually posts.

**Why not tie it to your own account.** It is tempting to let the bot borrow your access, so
that whatever you can reach it can reach too. That is exactly what makes it dangerous: a key
that is you can do everything you can do, including to repositories that have nothing to do with
this project, and a mistake by an agent holding it is a mistake made as you. A separate account
with Write on four repositories can, at worst, be reverted with a `git revert`. The bot being
weaker than you is the point.

**If the token leaks**: revoke it on the bot's token page, make a new one, `gh auth login`
again. Nothing else in the project has to change, because nothing else holds it.

## Signing commits locally

```bash
git config core.hooksPath .githooks
git config user.name  "GateKit Thrall"
git config user.email "<the account's noreply address>"
```

`.githooks/prepare-commit-msg` then rewrites any assistant's co-author trailer to the bot's and
adds the signature to commits the bot authors, and leaves everyone else's commits alone. In
continuous integration, the `signature` job checks a pull request opened by the bot carries the
line, and that no commit names an assistant.
